question: The horror of the now daily shipwrecks in the Aegean sea is intensifying, with dozens of displaced individuals dead or missing, including women and young children. In the last few days alone, six children and two women lost their lives when a boat sank off the northern coast of Samos and the body of a man was found on Fara beach on the island of Lesvos, adding to a long list of victims.

These incidents are linked to the current landscape in which we are seeing hostilities escalate on two imperialist war fronts between NATO and capitalist Russia in Ukraine, as well as the genocide against the Palestinian people and the imperialist interventions in Lebanon and Syria.
The ink is barely dry on the EU’s reactionary migration pact yet talks have already begun concerning an even more barbaric set of measures. In view of the above: 1.

What is the Commission’s take on the fact that the continuous shipwrecks in the Aegean are the result of a tougher crackdown – clearly assisted by Frontex – in the context of the EU’s goals and targets for reducing ‘irregular migration flows’, its chosen name for Palestinian, Lebanese, Syrian and other displaced refugees?

What is its take on the call to grant asylum and ensure the safe movement of war victims to their country of choice, in accordance with the Geneva Refugee Convention, under the oversight of the EU, the UN and governments?
What view does it take of the fact that Syria is considered a ‘safe’ country for refugees to return to, based partly on the recent views intentionally expressed by certain governments?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (10.4.2025) Repeated migrant deaths at sea are a tragic reminder of the need for a comprehensive approach to migration management and renewed efforts to combat migrant smuggling. The EU supports Member States in migration management (e.g. through financial and operational support), with the objective of creating fair, efficient, and sustainable migration and asylum systems.

At the same time, it will continue its work on preventing dangerous journeys from taking place. This is done by addressing the root causes of irregular migration and by reinforcing the existing framework to combat organised criminal networks along migratory routes to the EU.

The granting of international protection must be carried out in line with the requirements set out in the Qualification Directive1 which will be succeeded by the Qualification Regulation2 and reflects the Geneva Convention3. Both the Geneva Convention and the EU asylum acquis, however, do not provide beneficiaries of international protection with the right to reside in their country of choice.

The European Council Conclusions of 19 December 20244 reaffirmed the need to achieve conditions for safe, voluntary and dignified returns to Syria, as defined by the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR). The Commission is constantly monitoring the situation in Syria and remains in contact with UNHCR.
